newsitem.title: USA: Washington state voters narrowly favor stadium.
newsitem.headline: Washington state voters narrowly favor stadium.

text.p: A cliffhanger election on whether to build a new $425 million football stadium in Seattle tipped early Wednesday narrowly in favour of stadium supporters, who predicted a come-from-behind victory.
With 90 percent of the votes counted in the special election, election officials said 51 percent of the ballots were cast in favour of the controversial stadium project while 49 percent were opposed.
Supporters were ahead by just over 16,000 votes, a narrow margin given the number of ballots that remained to be counted. Earlier returns had suggested the project would be defeated.
The heated stadium election pitted well-funded supporters, backed by billionaire Paul Allen, against cash-strapped opponents, who had recruited consumer activist Ralph Nader.
Despite the narrow margin, stadium supporters said they were confident they would win the election.
"The final votes are not yet in," Allen said. "However, our projections show us ahead. The trend is positive."
Opponents would not concede, saying the election was still too close to call.

"The critical thing is that half the people in this state don't want stadiums paid for with public money when private companies are more than able to pay their own way," said Chris Van Dyk, a leading project opponent. "That's the message."

If approved, the proposal would provide about $325 million in public money for a 72,000-seat open-air stadium to house the Seattle Seahawks. Allen would invest an additional $100 million in the project. The new stadium would replace the ageing Kingdome, which would be demolished.
The deal was designed to keep the Seahawks in Seattle.
Allen, worth more than $13 billion as co-founder of Microsoft Corp., has offered to buy the team -- but only if the stadium referendum was approved.
Stadium proponents have argued that the Kingdome lacks the amenities to be profitable.
Opponents have countered that public funds should be used instead for roads, schools and public safety.

The stadium financing package would include $101 million from existing sales taxes, $127 million from lottery games, $56 million in stadium admissions and parking taxes, and $40 million in hotel room taxes.
The state of Washington would be authorised to issue up to $300 million of bonds to pay for site acquisition, design and construction of the stadium and an exhibition centre.
Allen has agreed to contribute $50 million of his own money plus $50 million from the sale of seat licenses -- permanent rights to seats -- as well as to cover any cost overruns.
Construction on the new stadium would start in the year 2000 and take two years. Demolition of the Kingdome would begin in late 1999.

Allen, who counts the Portland Trail Blazers basketball team among his many holdings, emerged as a white knight in April 1996 when he bought an option on the Seahawks to keep the team from being moved out of town.
He also paid for the six-week stadium campaign, which cost more than $4 million.
Opponents were able to raise only about $200,000 for a few cable television ads.

Similar stadium measures have appeared on local ballots across the United States in recent years. Many of these proposals have met stiff resistance from voters wary to commit public funds to sports projects.
Earlier this month a stadium proposal in San Francisco was approved, but only by the slimmest of margins.
